data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for the better-corroborated theory inevitably smuggles in induction because any decision to act based on past test results presupposes a principle of the uniformity of nature or the reliability of corroboration as a guide to future performance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent can demonstrate a purely logical link between surviving tests and future utility without assuming nature's uniformity, the claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' is redefined strictly as 'subjecting to further tests' and not 'relying on for practical outcomes', the inductive leap is avoided.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Pragmatic necessity forces the agent to assume that a theory that worked before will work again (or is less likely to fail) when building bridges or administering medicine. This assumption is inductive in structure, even if labeled 'corroboration'.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
